introduction: Where is the soul? The readings answer that the question is wrongly framed. The soul is not in the body as water is in a jug, and the Kingdom is not a place; “entering,” “leaving,” “ascending” are words for bodies. The soul is related to the body as the sun is to a mirror. It cannot be seen, weighed or located, and it is known by its effects: thought, discovery, the mastery of the body. Its essence cannot be known even by itself, and whatever is said of it “is but a drop.” Bahá’u’lláh calls it “a sign among the signs of God” that the wise have failed to comprehend, and adds that every soul is new. The outside texts include the Qur’án’s verse on the Spirit, Paul on the seen and the unseen and the spiritual body, the Upanishads, Augustine and Rúmí. The opposing views are among the best philosophy has produced: Aristotle’s wax and its shape, the lyre and its harmony from Plato’s Phaedo, Lucretius on the mind’s mortality, Hume’s search for a self, Plato’s own image of the body as a prison (which the readings also decline), and the Gita on rebirth.
questions: “The human body is in space; the soul has no place in space.” What everyday ways of speaking about the soul does this rule out? What is left to say?

The lyre and its harmony: when the instrument breaks, the music stops. State the objection as strongly as you can, and then ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reply with the sun and the mirror. Which facts does each explain?
Plato calls the body the soul’s prison; the readings deny that the soul is in the body at all. How might the two views lead to different attitudes toward the body and the world?
“To know the reality or essence of the soul of man is impossible,” because a thing cannot comprehend itself. Hume could not find himself by looking. Are these the same observation?
The soul is known through its effects. List the effects the readings name. Would any of them persuade someone who doubted?
“All … are new souls.” The Gita teaches rebirth. What is at stake between them for how one understands justice, suffering and the worth of a single life?

outside.why: “Nowhere do we see a spirit in man,” say the modern philosophers. A father in the Chandogya Upanishad has his son split a fig seed until nothing can be seen: that subtile essence which you do not perceive there, of that very essence this great Nyagrodha tree exists.
Hamlet to his learned friend: there are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.

The divine philosophers hold that the spirit is a reality distinct from the body. Aristotle, no materialist, thought the question badly put: it is as meaningless as to ask whether the wax and the shape given to it by the stamp are one. If the soul is the form of a living body, can it be without one? What do the readings say that Aristotle does not?
In man “are potentially revealed all the attributes and names of God.” A psalm: I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
Genesis: the Lord God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

What can be said of the soul “is but a drop from the surging ocean … It cannot be fully explained.” Augustine felt this about a thing as familiar as time: if no one ask of me, I know; if I wish to explain to him who asks, I know not.
“The Kingdom is not a material location.” Jesus: neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you.
Solomon, dedicating a temple: behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
“The soul has no place in space.” A psalm on a presence that is nowhere and everywhere: whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence?

The body is in space; the soul is not. Whitman would not have them parted: and if the body were not the soul, what is the soul? What is lost, in his view, by placing the real person outside the body, and what do the readings think is lost by placing it within?
“Some say: ‘We cannot see the soul.’” Jesus’ comparison: the wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth.

The spirit is hidden, yet “its commandments shine out like rays of light upon … the human body.” Paul reasons in the same way about God: the invisible things of him are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
An “inner reality” that does the discovering. Paul: though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
The ether, nature, and the human spirit are intelligible and not sensible realities. Paul: the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.
“With the help of our thoughts we can see other lands.” Emily Dickinson: the brain is wider than the sky, for, put them side by side, the one the other will include.
“The soul acts in the physical world with the help of the body.” The Katha Upanishad: know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot.

The spirit “is independent of the body.” In Plato’s Phaedo a friend of Socrates raises the strongest objection: harmony is invisible, incorporeal, fair, divine, yet when the lyre is broken the harmony perishes. Might the soul be to the body as music is to the instrument? How does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s image of the sun and the mirror answer?
Jesus assumes the independence when he speaks to those facing death: fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.

“Can I measure, weigh, touch, prove your soul?” Hume tried introspection and found only passing perceptions: I never can catch myself at any time without a perception. Is his failure evidence against the soul, or what the readings would expect?
We know things by “their attributes and not … their essence.” Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part.
If even created things are unknown in essence, how the Divinity? The Book of Job: canst thou by searching find out God?

It is hard to speak of the Kingdom so that “finite minds … grasp a faint conception.” Paul: eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared.
The spirit “has no likeness” in this world; it “is beyond explanation.” Isaiah says the same of its Source: to whom then will ye liken me, or shall I be equal? saith the Holy One.

Beyond explanation. Wittgenstein closed his first book with a rule: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá goes on speaking, by comparison and by pointing to effects. What can be said about what cannot be described?
The Chandogya Upanishad’s way of speaking of it: that subtile essence, in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou art it.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains “Paul’s statement that man has two bodies.” The statement: it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.
“Whatever is spoken or written cannot interpret the secrets of hearts.” Paul: the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered.
“I know not how to remember Thee.” A psalm: such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I cannot attain unto it.

The soul is “a divine sign … which all the learned have failed to comprehend.” The Qur’án: they will ask thee concerning the Spirit. Say: the Spirit is by command of my Lord, and of knowledge ye have been vouchsafed but little.
“A sign among the signs of God.” Proverbs: the spirit of man is the candle of the Lord.

“It cannot be said that the subtle spirit hath entered into … the body.” Plato said very nearly that: the soul is fastened and glued to the body, and views existence through the bars of a prison. Why do the readings refuse the picture of a prisoner inside a cell, and what does the refusal change in how the body is regarded?

Entering, leaving, ascending and descending belong to bodies. Marvell’s Soul complains as if it were locked in: with bolts of bones, that fetter’d stands in feet; and manacled in hands. If such language is figurative, what experience is it a figure for?

The spirit is related to the body “like … the sun with the mirror,” and is not contained in it. Paul uses a relation without location for God and ourselves: in him we live, and move, and have our being.

The soul does not depend on the body’s parts and needs no support when they decompose. Ecclesiastes: then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

The soul outlasts the body. Lucretius argued that mind grows, sickens and ages with the body and so ends with it: nothing to us was all the time before our birth. What do the readings do with the fact that the mind’s powers do visibly decline?
“The rational soul by which humans are distinguished from animals.” Job: there is a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding.
The spirit is hidden “yet rules over the body.” Jesus on its worth: what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
The human spirit “encompasses all things.” Pascal: by space the universe encompasses and swallows me up like an atom; by thought I comprehend the world.
“To know the reality or essence of the soul of man is impossible.” Deuteronomy: the secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us.
“All those called into being are new souls. It is not that a former soul becometh incarnated in another person.” The Letter to the Hebrews: it is appointed unto men once to die.

The Bhagavad Gita teaches the contrary with great beauty: as when one layeth his worn-out robes away, so putteth by the spirit lightly its garb of flesh, and passeth to inherit a residence afresh. Both teachings hold that the soul survives. What does each make of this one life?

Bahá’u’lláh quotes a Persian verse: “The rest of this tale comes without words.” The opening of Rúmí’s Masnaví is about the same wordless telling: hearken to the reed-flute, how it complains, lamenting its banishment from its home.
